questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Units of measurement and systems of units
questions.question: The light year is a unit of

solution.key_concept: A light year is the distance light travels in one year. It is a practical unit of astronomical distance.
steps: 1 light year $= 9.46 \times 10^{15}$ m.
This value is a length, so the light year measures distance.
solution.why_not_others: The word 'year' tempts students to choose time. Velocity would need length per time. Luminous intensity is measured in candela.
solution.common_trap: Treating the light year as a unit of time because of the word 'year'.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Units of measurement and systems of units
questions.question: A length measures 50 units when a unit $u$ is used. If a new unit equal to $2.5u$ is chosen, the numerical value of the same length becomes

solution.key_concept: Since $Q = n_1u_1 = n_2u_2$, the numerical value is inversely proportional to the size of the unit.
solution.why_not_others: 125 comes from multiplying by 2.5 instead of dividing. 52.5 and 47.5 come from adding or subtracting 2.5.
solution.common_trap: Thinking a bigger unit gives a bigger number.
solution.time_saving_tip: Bigger unit means smaller number, so divide.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Units of measurement and systems of units
questions.question: Using 1 parsec $\approx 3.08 \times 10^{16}$ m and 1 AU $\approx 1.496 \times 10^{11}$ m, the number of astronomical units in one parsec is approximately

solution.key_concept: Use $Q = n_1u_1 = n_2u_2$ to convert a distance from parsec to AU.
steps: Number of AU in 1 parsec $= \frac{3.08 \times 10^{16}}{1.496 \times 10^{11}}$.
This ratio $\approx 2.06 \times 10^{5}$.
solution.why_not_others: 3.26 is the number of light years in a parsec. $6.32 \times 10^{4}$ is the number of AU in a light year. $3.08 \times 10^{16}$ is the number of metres in a parsec.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the parsec-to-light-year ratio with the parsec-to-AU ratio.
solution.time_saving_tip: Approximate the ratio as $3/1.5 = 2$, which gives $2 \times 10^{5}$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Units of measurement and systems of units
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: When a physical quantity is expressed in a smaller unit, its numerical value becomes larger.
statements.R: The magnitude of a physical quantity depends on the system of units in which it is expressed.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Since $Q = nu$ is the same in every system, $n \propto \frac{1}{u}$.
steps: The quantity $Q$ is fixed, so a smaller $u$ needs a larger $n$. A is true.
The magnitude $Q$ itself does not change with the unit system. R is false.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A is true but R is false
solution.why_not_others: R contradicts $n_1u_1 = n_2u_2$. Only the numerical value changes, not the magnitude, so options (1), (2) and (4) fail.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the numerical value with the magnitude of the quantity.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Units of measurement and systems of units
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.II: The distance at which a length of 1 AU subtends an angle of one arcsecond is about $3.08 \times 10^{16}$ m.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Use 1 angstrom $= 10^{-10}$ m, 1 fermi $= 10^{-15}$ m, and the definition of the parsec.
steps: $\frac{1\ \text{angstrom}}{1\ \text{fermi}} = \frac{10^{-10}}{10^{-15}} = 10^{5}$, so 1 angstrom $= 10^{5}$ fermi. Statement I is incorrect.
1 parsec $= \frac{1\ \text{AU}}{1''} \approx 3.08 \times 10^{16}$ m. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: Statement I misses the true factor by $10^{2}$, so any option calling it correct fails. Statement II is the definition of the parsec, so any option calling it incorrect fails.
solution.common_trap: Subtracting the exponents wrongly when comparing $10^{-10}$ with $10^{-15}$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.question: The number of significant figures in 0.03060 is

solution.key_concept: Leading zeros are not significant. Zeros between non-zero digits and trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant.
steps: Drop the leading zeros '0.0'.
The remaining digits 3, 0, 6, 0 are all significant, giving 4.
solution.why_not_others: 3 ignores the trailing zero. 6 counts every digit including the leading zeros. 2 counts only the non-zero digits.
solution.common_trap: Counting leading zeros as significant.

questions.subject: physics
questions.question: In a vernier caliper, 1 MSD = 1 mm and 10 vernier divisions coincide with 9 main scale divisions. The instrument has a positive zero error of $+0.3$ mm. While measuring a rod, the main scale reading is 24 mm and the 7th vernier division coincides. The corrected length of the rod is

solution.key_concept: Use $LC = \frac{s}{n}$ and Reading $= MSR + VSR \times LC - \text{zero error}$.
steps: $LC = \frac{1\ \text{mm}}{10} = 0.1$ mm
Observed reading $= 24 + 7 \times 0.1 = 24.7$ mm
Corrected reading $= 24.7 - 0.3 = 24.4$ mm
solution.why_not_others: 25.0 mm adds the zero error. 24.7 mm ignores the zero error. 24.07 mm uses a least count of 0.01 mm.
solution.common_trap: Adding a positive zero error instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: physics
questions.question: The sum $12.4 + 2.356 + 0.07$, written with the correct number of significant figures, is

solution.key_concept: In addition, the result keeps the least number of decimal places among the terms.
steps: The raw sum is 14.826.
The fewest decimal places is one, in 12.4.
Rounding to one decimal place gives 14.8.
solution.why_not_others: 14.83 and 14.826 keep too many decimal places. 15 wrongly applies the significant-figure rule for multiplication.
solution.common_trap: Applying the multiplication rule to addition.

questions.subject: physics
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: In calculating the circumference $2\pi r$ from a measured radius, the factor 2 does not limit the number of significant figures of the result.
statements.R: The number 2 has only one significant figure.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Exact numbers have infinite significant figures.
steps: The 2 in $2\pi r$ is exact, so it does not restrict the precision of the result. A is true.
An exact number has infinitely many significant figures, not one. R is false.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A is true but R is false
solution.why_not_others: If R were true, the 2 would limit the result to one significant figure and A would be false. So R cannot be true alongside A.
solution.common_trap: Treating exact counting numbers like measured values.

questions.subject: physics
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: Rounding 6.735 to three significant figures gives 6.74.
statements.II: Rounding 4.865 to three significant figures gives 4.87.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: When the dropped digit is exactly 5, the preceding digit is raised only if it is odd.
steps: In 6.735 the preceding digit is 3, which is odd, so it rises to 4. The result 6.74 is correct.
In 4.865 the preceding digit is 6, which is even, so it stays. The result is 4.86, not 4.87.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Always rounding 5 up would make II correct. Always dropping 5 would make I incorrect. The odd-even rule gives option (3) only.
solution.common_trap: Always rounding up when the dropped digit is 5.

questions.subject: physics
questions.question: Which type of error can be reduced by taking the mean of a large number of observations?

solution.key_concept: Random errors fluctuate irregularly, so averaging many readings reduces them.
steps: Systematic errors act in one direction, so averaging does not remove them.
Random errors scatter on both sides of the true value, so they partly cancel in the mean.
solution.why_not_others: Zero error and instrumental error are both systematic and need correction or better technique, not repetition.
solution.common_trap: Believing that repetition removes all kinds of error.

questions.subject: physics
questions.question: Two lengths are $A = (50.0 \pm 0.3)$ cm and $B = (20.0 \pm 0.2)$ cm. The difference $A - B$ with its maximum error is

solution.key_concept: For $Z = A - B$, the maximum absolute error is $\Delta Z = \Delta A + \Delta B$.
solution.why_not_others: $\pm 0.1$ subtracts the errors. $\pm 0.36$ combines the errors in quadrature, which is not the maximum error. 70.0 adds the lengths instead of subtracting them.
solution.common_trap: Subtracting the errors when the quantities are subtracted.

questions.subject: physics
questions.question: A quantity is given by $Z = \frac{A^{2}B^{3}}{\sqrt{C}}$. The percentage errors in A, B and C are 1%, 2% and 4% respectively. The maximum percentage error in Z is

solution.key_concept: The percentage error in Z is the sum of (power) × (percentage error) for each quantity.
steps: Contribution of A: $2 \times 1\% = 2\%$
Contribution of B: $3 \times 2\% = 6\%$
Contribution of C: $\frac{1}{2} \times 4\% = 2\%$
solution.why_not_others: 7% ignores the powers. 6% subtracts the error of C because C is in the denominator. 16% uses a power of 2 for C instead of $\frac{1}{2}$.
solution.common_trap: Subtracting the error of a quantity that appears in the denominator.

questions.subject: physics
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_II.label: I
list_II.text: Fluctuates irregularly and is reduced by averaging many readings

list_II.label: II
list_II.text: Arises from carelessness of the observer

list_II.label: III
list_II.text: Resolution or repeatability of a measurement

list_II.label: IV
list_II.text: Acts in one direction, for example zero error

solution.key_concept: These are the definitions of the types of error and of precision.
steps: Systematic error acts in one direction (IV).
Random error fluctuates irregularly and is reduced by averaging (I).
Gross error comes from carelessness (II).
Precision is resolution or repeatability (III).
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) swaps systematic and random error. Option (2) swaps random and gross error. Option (3) swaps systematic error and precision.
solution.common_trap: Confusing systematic error with random error.

questions.subject: physics
questions.question: The period of a pendulum is measured five times as 2.62 s, 2.64 s, 2.60 s, 2.66 s and 2.63 s. Which of the following statements are correct?

statements.B: The mean absolute error is 0.016 s.
statements.D: Taking more readings will reduce any systematic error in the measurement.

solution.key_concept: Calculate the mean, then the mean absolute error, then the percentage error. Repetition reduces only random error.
steps: Mean $= \frac{13.15}{5} = 2.63$ s, so A is true.
The absolute errors are 0.01, 0.01, 0.03, 0.03 and 0.00 s. Their sum is 0.08 s, so the mean is $\frac{0.08}{5} = 0.016$ s. B is true.
Percentage error $= \frac{0.016}{2.63} \times 100 \approx 0.61\%$, so C is true.
Repetition does not reduce systematic error, so D is false.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A, B and C only
solution.why_not_others: Options (2) and (3) include the false statement D. Option (1) leaves out the true statement C.
solution.common_trap: Believing that more readings reduce systematic error.

questions.subject: physics
questions.question: Which of the following physical quantities has the same dimensions as the spring constant?

solution.key_concept: Spring constant is force per unit length, and surface tension is also force per unit length. Both have dimensions $[MT^{-2}]$.
steps: Spring constant: $k = F/x$, so $[k] = [MLT^{-2}]/[L] = [MT^{-2}]$.
Surface tension: force per unit length, so its dimensions are $[MT^{-2}]$.
Pressure is $[ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$, force is $[MLT^{-2}]$ and work is $[ML^2T^{-2}]$.
solution.why_not_others: Pressure is force per area, $[ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$. Force is $[MLT^{-2}]$. Work is force times distance, $[ML^2T^{-2}]$. None of these equals $[MT^{-2}]$.
solution.common_trap: Confusing force per unit length (surface tension, spring constant) with force per unit area (pressure).
solution.time_saving_tip: Remember the pair: surface tension and spring constant share $[MT^{-2}]$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.question: If $h$ is Planck's constant and $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant, the dimensions of $\frac{h}{k_B}$ are:

solution.key_concept: Use $[h] = [ML^2T^{-1}]$ and $[k_B] = [ML^2T^{-2}K^{-1}]$. The value of $k_B$ follows from $E = k_B T$.
solution.why_not_others: $[T^{-1}K^{-1}]$ is the dimension of $k_B/h$, which is the ratio inverted. $[TK^{-1}]$ and $[T^{-1}K]$ each come from a sign slip in one exponent.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting that dividing by $K^{-1}$ puts $K$ in the numerator.
solution.time_saving_tip: $M$ and $L^2$ cancel at once, so track only $T$ and $K$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.question: If $\mu_0$ is the permeability and $\epsilon_0$ is the permittivity of free space, the dimensions of the product $\mu_0\epsilon_0$ are:

solution.key_concept: $\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}} = c$, so $\mu_0\epsilon_0 = 1/c^2$.
steps: Adding the powers gives $M^0 L^{-2} T^{2} A^0$.
Check: $1/c^2$ has dimensions $[L^{-2}T^{2}]$, which agrees.
solution.why_not_others: $[L^2T^{-2}]$ is the dimension of $c^2$, which is the reciprocal. $[LT^{-1}]$ is the dimension of $c$, the value of $1/\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}$. $[L^{-1}T]$ is the dimension of $\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}$.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up $\mu_0\epsilon_0$ with $1/\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}$, which is the speed of light.
solution.time_saving_tip: Use $\mu_0\epsilon_0 = 1/c^2$ directly instead of multiplying the full formulas.

questions.subject: physics
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.R: Strain is the ratio of two similar quantities, change in length and original length.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: A ratio of two similar quantities is dimensionless.
steps: Strain $= \Delta l / l$, which is a length divided by a length.
So its dimensions are $[L]/[L]$, which gives no dimensions.
A is true because R is true, so R correctly explains A.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are true, so options (3) and (4) are ruled out. R is the direct reason strain has no dimensions, so option (2) is also wrong.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that strain, like stress, has the dimensions of pressure.

questions.subject: physics
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: The Boltzmann constant $k_B$ and the universal gas constant $R$ have identical dimensions $[ML^2T^{-2}K^{-1}]$.
statements.II: Magnetic flux has the dimensions $[MT^{-2}A^{-1}]$ and Wien's constant has the dimensions $[LK^{-1}]$.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Recall the exact dimensions of $k_B$, $R$, magnetic flux, magnetic field and Wien's constant.
steps: $[k_B] = [ML^2T^{-2}K^{-1}]$ but $[R] = [ML^2T^{-2}K^{-1}mol^{-1}]$. They are not identical, so I is incorrect.
$[MT^{-2}A^{-1}]$ is the dimension of magnetic field B. Magnetic flux is $[ML^2T^{-2}A^{-1}]$.
From $\lambda_m T = b$, $[b] = [LK]$, not $[LK^{-1}]$. So II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement I misses the $mol^{-1}$ in R. Statement II gives the dimensions of B instead of flux and inverts the power of K in Wien's constant.
solution.common_trap: Treating $k_B$ and $R$ as dimensionally identical, and confusing magnetic field with magnetic flux.
solution.time_saving_tip: Flux = B times area, so it carries an extra $L^2$ compared with B.

questions.subject: physics
questions.question: A wave is described by $y = A\sin(\omega t - kx)$, where $x$ is a distance and $t$ is time. The dimensions of $k$ are:

solution.key_concept: The argument of $\sin$ must be dimensionless.
steps: $kx$ must be dimensionless.
solution.why_not_others: $[L]$ inverts the result. $[T^{-1}]$ is the dimension of $\omega$. $[LT^{-1}]$ is the dimension of wave speed $\omega/k$.
solution.common_trap: Assigning the dimensions of $\omega$ to $k$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.question: In a new system of units, the unit of mass is 100 g, the unit of length is 10 cm and the unit of time is 1 s. A force of 10 N, expressed in this system, has the numerical value:

steps: $n_2 = 10 \times 10 \times 10 \times 1 = 1000$.
solution.why_not_others: 100 uses only one of the two factors of 10. 10 assumes the value is unchanged. 0.1 comes from inverting the ratios to $M_2/M_1$ and $L_2/L_1$.
solution.common_trap: Writing the ratios as new unit over old unit instead of old over new.
solution.time_saving_tip: Smaller units always give a larger numerical value.

questions.subject: physics
questions.question: In the equation $\left(P + \frac{a}{V^2}\right)(V - b) = RT$, $P$ is pressure and $V$ is volume. The dimensions of $a$ are:

solution.key_concept: By the principle of homogeneity, $\frac{a}{V^2}$ must have the dimensions of pressure.
solution.why_not_others: $[ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$ is the dimension of $P$ itself. $[ML^{-7}T^{-2}]$ comes from dividing by $V^2$ instead of multiplying. $[L^6]$ is the dimension of $V^2$ alone.
solution.common_trap: Dividing pressure by $V^2$ instead of multiplying.

questions.subject: physics
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: $\omega$ in $y = A\sin(\omega t - kx)$, $t$ being time

solution.key_concept: Use homogeneity and the rule that the arguments of $\sin$ and $\exp$ are dimensionless.
steps: A: $\omega t$ is dimensionless, so $[\omega] = [T^{-1}]$, which is I.
B: $[a] = [P][V^2] = [ML^5T^{-2}]$, which is II.
C: $bx$ is dimensionless, so $[b] = [L^{-1}]$. Then $[a] = [P][b] = [ML^{-2}T^{-2}]$, which is IV.
D: $[l/g] = [L]/[LT^{-2}] = [T^2]$, which is III.
solution.why_not_others: Option (2) swaps the two different constants named $a$. Option (3) swaps the dimensions of $\omega$ and $l/g$. Option (4) confuses $[T^2]$ with $[ML^{-2}T^{-2}]$.
solution.common_trap: In C, taking $a$ to have the dimensions of $P$ while forgetting the factor $1/b$.
solution.time_saving_tip: D must be $[T^2]$ because $T \propto \sqrt{l/g}$. That alone eliminates options (3) and (4).

questions.subject: physics
questions.question: Which of the following statements about dimensional analysis are correct?

statements.A: It cannot determine the dimensionless constant $2\pi$ in $T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$.
statements.B: It cannot tell whether a physical quantity is a scalar or a vector.
statements.C: An equation that is dimensionally correct must also be physically correct.
statements.D: It can be used to derive relations involving exponential functions.
statements.E: Only quantities having the same dimensions can be added or subtracted.

solution.key_concept: Know the uses and the limitations of dimensional analysis.
steps: A is true: dimensionless constants cannot be found.
B is true: the method gives no information about direction.
C is false: a wrong numerical factor still passes the dimensional check.
D is false: relations with $\sin$, $\log$ or exponential functions cannot be derived.
E is true: this is the principle of homogeneity.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A, B and E only
solution.why_not_others: Options (2) and (4) include C, which is false. Option (3) includes D, which is false.
solution.common_trap: Believing that passing the dimensional check proves an equation is correct.
solution.time_saving_tip: Spot C as false first. That eliminates options (2) and (4) at once.
